newsitem.title: DUBAI: South African miners need to make more use of hedging - analyst.
newsitem.headline: South African miners need to make more use of hedging - analyst.

text.p: South African gold mining firms should make greater use of hedging on forward markets to protect their margins against weak international bullion prices, an equities analyst said on Sunday.

"Higher cost producers, and that really is the South African industry, should have a stronger motivation to hedge and thus protect thin margins," said Ted Reeve, equities analyst at Canada's Scotia McLeod Inc.

Only 10 to 15 percent of gold output in South Africa, the world's largest producer with an annual output of 500 tonnes, was currently delivered against hedge contracts and even then policy was conservative.

"Among the six (South African) mining houses really only Anglo American makes use of the forward markets to hedge, with less than 10 months of production hedged, below the level of all but the smallest of Australian producers," Reeve told delegates at a gold conference in Dubai.
In contrast, major gold producers in Australia and North America hedged their future sales more extensively, as far as 2009, and had secured higher returns despite weak gold prices.
Australia has hedged 890 tonnes, compared with annual production of 290 tonnes, and North American mining firms had 870 tonnes hedged on total output of 490 tonnes.

"As of year-end 1996 the Australian industry is looking forward to receiving an average gold price of $512 an ounce for contracts which extend from now until well on into the second half of the decade," Reeve told delegates.
North American mines had nearly 40 percent and 31 percent of their output hedged in each of the next two years at over $400.
International bullion was last quoted on Saturday at $342.20/$342.70 an ounce, close to its lowest level since 1993.
The need to protect margins was highlighted this month when lower gold prices and a stronger rand hit first quarter results at South African mining houses.

"I believe that there is room for substantial increases in hedging by South African companies and even to reach North American levels...(but) for this to happen we need first a change in policy by the South African producers," said Reeve.
